sentences.label: Lowering the chance
sentences.text: These add up independently, and these lower the chance: a higher education level lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) steadily, from about 89% at 7 to about 24% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, flattening out near the top because the predicted chance cannot go much higher, and higher capital losses (about 62% at 0 to about 29% at 1887 US dollars) and longer working hours (about 71% at 24 to about 52% at 55 hours a week) lower it steadily.

Being a wife rather than a husband lowers it to about 27%; through this sum alone, a highest education of 1st-4th grade lowers it to about 10%, 7th-8th grade to about 19%, and being born in Ireland to about 26% (highest education and country of birth also act through the parts below).

sentences.label: Raising the chance
sentences.text: Being a child of the household rather than a husband raises it to about 94%, a marital status other than married to a civilian to about 87% and being a woman to about 80%; a missing work class raises it to about 79%, and through this sum alone farming or fishing raises it to about 83%, other service work to about 81% and being born in Vietnam to about 87% (occupation also acts through the parts below).

sentences.label: Rare results
sentences.text: Through this sum alone, being born in Scotland raises it to about 88% and being born in Honduras lowers it to about 43% (the model has little data on this, n = 16 and 14).

Through this part, higher capital gains lower a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) slowly at first, then faster: from about 62% at 0 to about 6% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.

Through this part, older age lowers a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) steadily up to about 35 years, then no further: from about 93% at 22 to about 62% at 58 years.

Through this part, handling or cleaning raises a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 62% to about 76%, while a doctorate lowers it to about 52% and being born in Cambodia to about 52% (the model has little data on this, n = 19).

This part acts only on the 187 people in private household service, 185 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; through it, such work raises a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 62% to about 87%.

Through this part, a technical-support job lowers a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 62% to about 52%, while being born in Guatemala or a missing country of birth raises it a little, to about 65%.

This part acts only on the 96 people born in China, 68 of whom have an income of $50,000 or less; through it, being born in China raises a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 62% to about 85%.
Through this part, being Asian or Pacific Islander lowers a typical person's predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) a little, from about 62% to about 58%.

lead.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week, with no capital gains or losses) the model predicts a chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) of about 62%; it adds up most of the person's characteristics independently, and seven parts add to that sum.

evidence.text: It consists of the inputs that feed the score directly and seven parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, checked on all 39073 training people.

When one input at a time is changed across the whole model, a higher education level takes a typical person's chance steadily from about 89% at 7 to about 24% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, flattening out near the top because the predicted chance cannot go much higher, and higher capital gains lower it slowly at first, then faster, from about 62% at 0 to about 6% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.
Looking at the whole model, a highest education of 1st-4th grade lowers it to about 10% and 7th-8th grade to about 19%, and being born in Ireland to about 26%.

Looking at the whole model, being a child of the household raises it to about 94% and private household service rather than a professional job to about 87%, while being a wife rather than a husband lowers it to about 27%.

parts.name: income_logit
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: the network is an additive logistic model. logit P(<=50K) = 0.776 + sparse linear backbone over 40 direct inputs + sum of 7 child contributions, then sigmoid. Backbone (direct edges, standardised inputs): education-num -1.41, marital-status:2 (Married-civ-spouse) -0.73, relationship:5 (Wife) -0.56, relationship:0 (Husband) -0.56, relationship:3 (Own-child) +0.43, sex (Male) -0.42, hours-per-week -0.33, capital-loss -0.30, plus small workclass/occupation/education/country offsets. Children: capital_gain_penalty (concave piecewise-linear, kink ~5.2k USD), youth_hinge (+0.16 logit per year below ~35), and five near-inert categorical gates (Handlers-cleaners/Doctorate relay, Tech-support, Priv-house-serv, China, Asian-Pac offset). The children have no multiplicative interactions; they meet only at the output sum. 54 one-hot inputs are unconnected (zero effect); native-country:15 is constant in train; four hidden nodes (9712, 5394, 12643, 2197) never activate. Evidence: closed form (get_formula); train acc 0.852, AUC 0.908 (n=39073); local mean-ablations: backbone AUC->0.748, capital gain ->0.890, age ->0.900, each gate costs <=0.0003 AUC; KernelSHAP (200 train samples) top mean|SHAP|: education-num 0.105, marital-status:2 0.068, relationship:0 0.054, identity_age 0.046, identity_capgain 0.040, sex 0.026. Supported.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients
